source.title: Ultra-Dense Cell-Free Massive MIMO for 6G: Technical Overview and Open Questions

accepted.question_text: What practical, scalable radio-access-network architecture can support user-centric cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO), where many distributed access points (APs) coherently serve users without fixed cell boundaries and each user is served by a dynamically changing AP cluster, especially when those clusters must be controlled across Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) distributed units and fronthaul links as user load and locations change?

evidence.quote: Designing a scalable and practical architecture for CF-MMIMO is a major challenge.
However, the main challenge in user-centric CF-MMIMO is how to control the user-centric clusters.
So the key question is: what is a practical architecture to support user-centric CF-MMIMO?
However, the current O-RAN standard lacks a well-defined framework for the inter-O-DU coordination interface.

accepted.question_text: What user-centric signal-processing design should an ultra-dense cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) system use for uplink combining and downlink precoding when the alternatives include centralized processing at central processing units (CPUs), local processing at each access point (AP), and cluster-level combinations that trade spectral efficiency, fronthaul traffic, CPU computational load, robustness to AP additions or failures, and support for multiple-antenna APs?
accepted.context_brief: Choice of centralized, local, or hybrid processing

evidence.quote: B. What User-Centric Processing Should Ultra-Dense Cell-Free Massive MIMO Use?
In Section IV, we described a general user-centric CF-MMIMO system where the signal processing, including UL combining and DL precoding, can be done centrally at the CPUs or locally at each AP.

In summary, local processing stands out as an ideal choice for ultra-dense CF-MMIMO systems. It provides an excellent balance between the computational complexity, system resilience, and system performance.
The remaining challenge in implementing this approach is the necessity for a flexible fronthaul infrastructure capable of dynamically routing fronthaul traffic among dynamic clusters.

accepted.question_text: How should a user-centric ultra-dense cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) network dynamically route uplink traffic from access points (APs) to central processing units (CPUs) and downlink traffic from CPUs to APs, place software-defined cluster processors on CPUs with finite computation capacity, and choose fronthaul quantization rates so that dynamic AP-user clusters remain scalable without overloading fronthaul links or computation resources?
accepted.context_brief: Fronthaul routing, processor placement, and quantization

evidence.quote: C. How to Dynamically Route Fronthaul Traffic and Quantize Signals?

As discussed in previous sections, since users are served by user-centric clusters of APs that depend on the user locations and are not a priori determined, a requirement for scalability is that APs and CPUs are connected by a flexible fronthaul network, able to route the data traffic between APs and CPUs.
For a given network topology, the load balancing (via routing) and the allocation of computation resources must be jointly optimized.
In order to optimize the UL fronthaul load, a critical aspect is the fronthaul quantization, i.e., the complex samples r u m,k are quantized with a finite number of bits.

accepted.question_text: Under what propagation, density, antenna, processing, and traffic conditions is the channel-hardening or use-and-then-forget bounding technique a reliable achievable-rate tool for cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO), and when should researchers instead use full-side-information bounds with downlink training, blind channel estimation, non-coherent bounds, enhanced normalized precoding, or scheduling changes?

evidence.quote: D. When Does the Hardening Bounding Technique Work?

In CF-MMIMO, since only a subset of APs serves a given user and the channels from different APs have different large-scale fading coefficients, the level of channel hardening may not be as pronounced.
In some practical scenarios, particularly in UDNs, channels from a given user to different APs may not be independent, and hence, the channel hardening is not guaranteed.
In these scenarios, more suitable bounding techniques become necessary and the associated channel acquisition schemes should be considered.

In some practical systems, especially with bursty traffic where the users have dynamic buffers, the user scheduling is done every transmission time interval (TTI) and over narrow frequency bands. Consequently, the set of active users changes quickly over time/frequency. In such cases, this bound may not be the most suitable approach.

accepted.question_text: How much prior channel information, especially access-point (AP)-user channel covariance matrices or dominant channel subspaces, is actually available in practical cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) deployments, and how should that information be estimated and used to mitigate pilot contamination without assuming unavailable global or uncontaminated channel statistics?
accepted.context_brief: Availability and use of channel statistics

evidence.quote: E. How Much Prior Information is Really Available and How Much Should be Used?
Pilot contamination can be mitigated by exploiting the knowledge of the channel statistics.
The channel covariance matrices (or dominant channel subspaces) for each AP-user pair (m, k) must also be estimated.
Nevertheless, the acquisition of the channel statistics is affected by the same pilot contamination problem that its use tries to defeat.

accepted.question_text: How can distributed access points (APs) in cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) be synchronized and reciprocity-calibrated in time, frequency, and phase with acceptable cost, signaling overhead, and disruption to time-division-duplex (TDD) operation, particularly when inexpensive oscillators may drift quickly and over-the-air calibration can require bidirectional AP measurements?

evidence.quote: Different kinds of synchronization are required for distributed APs to work together.
The time synchronization is comparatively easy, while alignment in phase can be more difficult.

The third option is to equip the APs with free-running oscillators; in this case, re-calibration for joint reciprocity is required every time the oscillators have drifted by more than some amount [116], [117].
Such over-the-air calibration obviates the need for synchronization cables, which are considered costly, but on the other hand imposes a substantial signaling load and disrupts the TDD flow

accepted.question_text: What role should uplink and downlink power control play in scalable cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO), and how can power-control methods balance sum spectral efficiency, fairness, near-far mitigation, interference control, centralization versus distribution, partial channel state information (CSI) sharing, and the practical limits of machine-learning or reinforcement-learning approaches?

evidence.quote: G. What is the Role of Power Control?
As in any wireless network, power allocation is important in CF-MMIMO to tackle the near-far effect and minimize the interference [14], [52].
Any non-trivial network-wide optimal power allocation is unscalable as the number of AP and/or users grows unboundedly.

To summarize, to preserve the scalability of the system, power control implementations should be either heuristic and fully distributed, or sub-optimal and centralized but requiring only partial CSI sharing.
Such techniques are thus unscalable and impractical.

accepted.question_text: How should massive machine-type communication (mMTC) be supported in cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) when many low-complexity devices transmit sporadically with very small packets, strict latency and reliability requirements, limited channel-coherence resources for orthogonal pilots, uncertain traffic patterns, and insufficient or costly channel state information?

evidence.quote: The accommodation of mMTC traffic in cellular networks brings new fundamental challenges [131].

As a consequence, in the massive MTC context, the signaling overhead makes many conventional techniques almost useless and new approaches to random access and the control plane, or even the data transmission, are required.
These are unsolved challenges that call for new solution techniques.

While approaches in the literature assume the availability of full or partial channel state information [133], in mMTC setups, the acquisition of channel state information requires the allocation of additional resources and it is also possible the assumed channel models do not capture the real characteristics of the transmission channels.

accepted.question_text: How can dynamic scheduling be implemented in user-centric cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) when the total user population greatly exceeds the number of users that can be active on each time-frequency resource block, coding and decoding occur block by block rather than over infinitely many fading states, scheduled rates must account for outage probability, pilot-contamination conflicts constrain simultaneous users, and long-term throughput should remain fair?

evidence.quote: I. How to Implement Dynamic Scheduling?
This assumption may be incompatible with dynamic scheduling and per-slot coding/decoding, as well as with low-latency requirements, which are key features of 5G [144], [145].

The scheduler must allocate an “instantaneous” rate to each active user since encoding/decoding is performed block by block, i.e., coding over a virtually infinite sequence of fading states is not possible.

The problem of dynamic scheduling in user-centric CF-MMIMO networks where the number of total users is much larger than the number of simultaneously active users on each time-frequency RB has not been widely investigated and remains quite open.

accepted.question_text: Which emerging physical infrastructure can realize cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) at scale, and how can Radio Stripes, pCell-like centralized distributed antenna systems, and RadioWeaves-style integrated distributed antennas overcome practical limits involving fronthaul capacity, data processing, synchronization, mobility, initial access, energy efficiency, and support for energy-neutral backscatter devices?

evidence.quote: CF-MMIMO requires a widespread and costly architecture to implement the user-centric philosophy, accurate synchronization and coordination among the APs to carry out the joint coherent transmission/reception, and practical resource allocation schemes to capitalize on the macro-diversity gain, while preserving the network scalability.
On the other hand, the Radio Stripe system cannot be the ideal solution for any large-scale distributed deployment.
It is fundamentally difficult in pCell, or any such CF-MMIMO system, to support substantial mobility, given the CSI and user-centered synchronization requirements.
One important technical challenge in constructing RadioWeaves system is, down-to-earth, to handle the vast amounts of baseband data, and process them in real time.
A fifth is the integration of service of energy-neutral devices that communicate via backscattering.

accepted.question_text: How can ultra-dense cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) implement low-complexity interference-suppression precoding and combining that cancels only the most significant intra-access-point (intra-AP) and inter-access-point (inter-AP) interference, avoids large pseudo-inverse computations, limits fronthaul overhead, and still approaches the performance of network-wide zero forcing or minimum mean-square error (MMSE)-style processing?

evidence.quote: 1) Low-complexity processing: When designing interference-suppression-based precoding and combining schemes, the complexity of implementing the beamforming vectors mainly lies in the computation of the pseudo-inverse matrix, hence on its size.
In CF-MMIMO, due to the distributed network topology, the dynamic range of the interference from/to different APs may be large.
These are fully distributed precoding schemes that provide an adaptable trade-off between interference cancellation and boosting of the desired signal, with no additional fronthaul overhead.

Such a joint MR transmission and ZF (JMRZF) precoding scheme converges to the performance of network-wide ZF as the number of APs included in the ZF set grows, at the expense of an increased computational complexity and fronthaul overhead.

accepted.question_text: How can cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) systems exchange or acquire the channel state information (CSI) needed for distributed cooperative precoding under tight time constraints while keeping the CSI-sharing overhead low-dimensional, avoiding fronthaul dominance, and preserving performance when access points (APs) may have transmitter-specific or delayed estimates of the global channel state?

evidence.quote: 2) Low-dimensional CSI exchange: Although the DCC framework allows to confine the data sharing among a subset of APs, hence relieving the fronthaul network, CSI sharing between the APs needs to be performed within much tighter time constraints, and hence may dominate the fronthaul overhead.
A viable approach to limit the CSI sharing consists in implementing cooperative transmission strategies only among a few APs.

On the other hand, [163] proposes a distributed framework for cooperative precoding in CF-MMIMO systems based on a novel over-the-air (OTA) signaling mechanism that entirely eliminates the need for fronthaul signaling for CSI exchange.
These practical benefits come at the cost of extra UL signaling overhead per bi-directional training iteration

accepted.question_text: How can ultra-dense cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) remain robust when low-cost hardware introduces phase noise, carrier-frequency offsets, analog-to-digital converter quantization noise, and power-amplifier nonlinearities, especially because nonlinear distortion can be correlated across distributed antennas, coherently combine at user locations, and create out-of-band emissions that strict standards may limit?

evidence.quote: 3) Robustness against hardware impairments: To keep down the costs of deploying an UDN, it is desirable to use inexpensive hardware.
Nevertheless, low-quality hardware may introduce distortion that causes significant system performance losses.
One consequence is that in most cases of practical relevance, the distortion is correlated among the antennas.
While DL precoders can be adapted to combat the effects of nonlinearities to some extent [167], [168], observing strict out-of-band emission requirements can be challenging.

If out-of-band radiation (the most difficult and important hardware impairment on DL) is of concern, then to meet out-of-band emission requirements one has to account for the worst case, in which case the uncorrelatedness-approximation is inapplicable and the rigorous analyses of [164]–[166] must be used.

accepted.question_text: At what level of access-point densification does cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) become truly beneficial for a wireless network, and under what deployment, propagation, interference, cost, or coverage conditions is CF-MMIMO not actually needed despite increasing network density?

evidence.quote: In addition to the key questions addressed in this paper, there are still many interesting research questions requiring future comprehensive studies, such as 1) At what level of densification is CF-MMIMO truly beneficial? When is it not really needed?
Without being able to communicate with multiple APs, the cell-free paradigm is impossible to achieve.

Without any effort to reduce interference, in many deployment and propagation scenarios, UDN networks can suffer from a “densification collapse”, meaning that both the SINR and even the sum throughput saturate and then tend to zero after a certain level of densification is reached

accepted.question_text: How can cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) support communication with backscattering or energy-neutral devices, including integration with simultaneous transmission and reception from different distributed panels, without breaking the time-division-duplex flow or compromising coherent cell-free operation?

When is it not really needed?; 2) How to handle high mobility in UDNs with CF-MMIMO?; 3) CF-MMIMO for communication with backscattering devices

CF-MMIMO naturally offers the infrastructure for that, permitting simultaneous transmission and reception from different panels in a bistatic setup; however, these activities break the TDD flow and must be carefully integrated into the workings of the system.

accepted.question_text: How does cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) work when users have multiple antennas rather than a single antenna, including channel estimation, dynamic scheduling procedures, and signal processing at the user terminals and distributed access points?

The system comprises M APs and K users distributed within a defined coverage area. Each AP is equipped with N antennas, while each user has a single antenna.
In addition, in LoS propagation environments, CF-MMIMO with multiple-antenna users can offer favorable propagation, but co-located massive MIMO may not.

accepted.question_text: How should cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MMIMO) be combined with other advanced 6G technologies, including reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, near-field transmissions, and artificial-intelligence methods, while preserving scalable channel estimation, scheduling, synchronization, signal processing, and resource allocation in ultra-dense deployments?
accepted.context_brief: CF-MMIMO with RIS, near-field, and AI

evidence.quote: In addition to the key questions addressed in this paper, there are still many interesting research questions requiring future comprehensive studies, such as 1) At what level of densification is CF-MMIMO truly beneficial? When is it not really needed?; 2) How to handle high mobility in UDNs with CF-MMIMO?; 3) CF-MMIMO for communication with backscattering devices; 4) How CF-MMIMO works (including channel estimation, scheduling procedures, signal processing at the users) with multiple-antenna users; and 5) How to combine CF-MMIMO with other advanced technologies such as reconfigurable intelligent surface, near-field transmissions, and AI technologies.
Furthermore, 6G is poised to enable new use cases stemming from advanced capabilities, particularly those related to artificial intelligence (AI) and multi-sensory interactions.
Importantly, RadioWeaves, and CF-MMIMO more generally, naturally operates in the [geometric] near-field of the “super-array” collectively constituted by all antenna panels together.
